title: Native pronunciation
theme: Word stress, sentence stress (content vs function words), weak forms (schwa), connected speech (linking, intrusive sounds, assimilation, elision), contractions, intonation
goal: Student speaks with native-like rhythm and stress — knowing which words to stress, which to weaken, and how to link sounds across word boundaries.
connects_to: M21 (Fala como nativo) — moves from sound shape to lexical and pragmatic native-like choices.
module_chunks: content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) = stressed
function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns) = weak/unstressed
weak forms with schwa: of /əv/, for /fə/, to /tə/, and /ən/, a /ə/, the /ðə/, you /jə/
contractions: he's, she's, we'd, they've, won't, can't, shouldn't, wouldn't
intonation: yes/no rise, wh-fall, statement fall, list rise-rise-fall

units.title: Word stress
units.grammar_focus: Word stress in multi-syllable words — especially noun/verb pairs (PROduce/proDUCE, CONtract/conTRACT) and Latinate words (phoTOgraphy, photoGRAphic)
units.real_life_context: You stress the right syllable so listeners parse the word without effort — wrong stress is one of the biggest comprehension blockers in C1+ speech.

grammar.sentence: Where is the stress in "photograph"?
grammar.explanation: "PHO-tograph" — stress on first syllable. Compare with "phoTOgraphy" (stress on second) and "photoGRAphic" (stress on third). The same root shifts stress based on the suffix. C2 mastery includes knowing how word formation shifts stress.

grammar.sentence: Noun-verb pair: which has stress on the first syllable as a noun?
grammar.explanation: Many two-syllable noun-verb pairs follow the pattern: NOUN stress on first, VERB stress on second. "REcord" (a recording, noun) vs "reCORD" (to record, verb). Similar pairs: PROduce / proDUCE, CONtract / conTRACT, OBject / obJECT, PERmit / perMIT. Native speakers signal the part of speech via stress.

grammar.sentence: Which syllable carries stress in "comfortable"? _____
grammar.explanation: "COMfortable" — stress on "COM". Native speakers often reduce to "COMF-tər-bəl" (three syllables in fast speech). Many learners stress "comFORTable" or "comforTABLE", which sounds foreign. C2 awareness includes the first-syllable stress on "comfortable" and similar long Latinate words.

grammar.sentence: Which is correct stress for "develop"?
grammar.explanation: "deVELop" — stress on second syllable. Pattern for similar verbs: deCIDE, reMEMber, beGIN, dis-COVer, sup-PORT. Two-or-three-syllable verbs often stress the second syllable (especially with prefixes de-, re-, dis-). Wrong stress in everyday verbs is a major C2 fluency leak.

grammar.passage: Stress shifts can change meaning entirely. PROduce (noun: vegetables and fruit) is different from proDUCE (verb: to make). PERmit (noun: a licence) differs from perMIT (verb: to allow). OBject (noun: a thing) sits opposite obJECT (verb: to oppose). For every misplaced stress, a momentary parse failure passes through the listener's mind.
grammar.question: What does the passage say happens when stress is misplaced?
grammar.answer: a momentary parse failure passes through the listener's mind
grammar.explanation: Three noun-verb pairs with stress contrast: PROduce/proDUCE, PERmit/perMIT, OBject/obJECT. Each pair shares spelling but differs in stress, and the stress signals the part of speech. C2 listeners hear this shift instantly; speakers must produce it.

listening_speaking.text: Take a PHO-tograph, study the phoTO-graphy, become photo-GRAphic.
REcord a podcast — but first, reCORD the file path.
This is a COMfortable chair — entirely COMfortable.
They deVELop software but DEvelopment takes time.
The PROduce was fresh; the team will proDUCE another batch.

units.title: Sentence stress and weak forms
units.grammar_focus: Content words (stressed) vs function words (weak/unstressed), schwa /ə/ in weak forms (of, for, to, and, a, the)
units.real_life_context: You speak with the rhythm of English — stressing meaning-carrying words and weakening grammar-glue words.

grammar.sentence: In the sentence "I want a cup of tea", which words are stressed?
grammar.answer: I, want, cup, tea (sometimes also "I" reduced)
grammar.explanation: Content words (nouns: cup, tea; verbs: want; sometimes pronouns: I) carry stress. Function words (a, of, the, am, is) weaken. In normal speech: "I WANT a CUP of TEA" with "a" and "of" reduced to schwa /ə/. Stress = meaning markers.

grammar.sentence: Weak form of "of" in connected speech:
grammar.explanation: "Of" weakens to /əv/ in normal speech — schwa + soft v. "Cup of tea" → "cupəv tea". Native speakers almost never say "OFF" with full stress unless contrasting ("It's of the BOOK, not from it"). Weak forms are nearly invisible but constant.

grammar.sentence: Identify weak form of "to": "I want to go" → "I want _____ go." (in connected fast speech)
grammar.explanation: "To" weakens to /tə/ in connected speech. "Want to" often blends into "wanna" /ˈwɒnə/ in casual register. C2 listeners parse "wanna / gonna / gotta" as "want to / going to / got to" — and produce them naturally in informal contexts.

grammar.sentence: Which sentence has the more native rhythm? "I AM going TO the STORE" or "I'm going to the STORE"?
grammar.hint: Native English weakens auxiliaries and uses contractions
grammar.explanation: Equal stress on every word ("I AM going TO the STORE") sounds robotic. Native rhythm contracts ("I'm") and weakens function words ("going tə the"). Only content words get full stress: "I'm GOing to the STORE". Stress-timed rhythm.

grammar.passage: English is stress-timed. The amount of time between stressed syllables stays roughly constant, no matter how many unstressed syllables sit between them. 'BEN went HOME' takes about the same time as 'BENjamin has GONE to the HOUSE' — the function words and unstressed syllables compress to keep the beat. Native rhythm is built on this compression.
grammar.question: How does English keep the same rhythm even with more words?
grammar.answer: by compressing function words and unstressed syllables between content words (stressed beats stay roughly evenly spaced)
grammar.explanation: Stress-timed language: the rhythm is set by stressed syllables, and everything else fits between them. Portuguese is syllable-timed (each syllable roughly equal); English compresses unstressed syllables. C2 spoken fluency = mastery of this compression.

listening_speaking.text: I WANT a CUP of TEA.

units.title: Connected speech
units.real_life_context: You connect sounds across word boundaries — the way fluent English actually runs together.

grammar.sentence: In natural speech, "an apple" sounds like:
grammar.explanation: Linking: when a word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, the consonant attaches to the next word in connected speech. "An apple" → "a-NAP-pl". "Stop it" → "sto-PIT". "Find out" → "fine-DOUT". Native rhythm relies on this linking.

grammar.sentence: "Law and order" in natural British English includes which intrusive sound?
grammar.explanation: Intrusive /r/: a sound inserted between two vowels where no "r" exists in spelling. "Law and order" → "law-r-and order". Common in British English. Same pattern: "drawing" → "draw-r-ing" (heard especially in fast speech). American English uses it less.

grammar.sentence: In fast connected speech, "I am" becomes "I-_-am" (intrusive sound)
grammar.explanation: Intrusive /j/: a "y" sound bridges two vowels. "I am" /aɪ-jæm/ "go away" /goʊ-wəweɪ/ uses intrusive /w/. These sounds aren't in spelling but native speakers produce them automatically to avoid awkward vowel-to-vowel transitions.

grammar.sentence: Which is closer to natural fast speech of "don't you know"?
grammar.explanation: Assimilation: when adjacent sounds change to be more similar. "Don't you" → "doncha" /ˈdoʊnʧə/. "Did you" → "didja" /ˈdɪʤə/. "Would you" → "wouldja". These aren't lazy — they're the natural shape of fast English. C2 awareness includes both producing and parsing them.

grammar.passage: Native English in flow rarely sounds like written English. 'I'm going to find out what he said' compresses to 'I'm-gonna-fine-DOUT what-he-SAID' — linking, weak forms, elision. The written words are unchanged. The sounds are barely recognisable to learners taught only the careful version. Connected speech is the gap between textbook and spoken English.
grammar.question: According to the passage, what is the gap between textbook and spoken English?
grammar.answer: connected speech (linking, weak forms, elision, assimilation that the textbook doesn't show)
grammar.explanation: Three phenomena named: linking (across word boundaries), weak forms (function-word reduction), elision (sound drops like /t/ in fast speech). All three are normal native pronunciation, but textbooks rarely show them, leaving learners surprised when they encounter real speech.

units.title: Intonation
units.grammar_focus: Intonation patterns — yes/no question rise, wh-question fall, statement fall, list rise-rise-fall, sarcasm/disbelief patterns
units.real_life_context: You signal meaning through pitch — questions, statements, lists, emotional nuance.

grammar.sentence: Typical intonation pattern for "Are you ready?":
grammar.explanation: Yes/no questions typically end with rising intonation. "Are you ready?" rises on "ready". Compare with wh-questions ("What time is it?") which fall on the last content word. Rising intonation signals expectation of yes/no answer.

grammar.sentence: Typical intonation for "What time is it?":
grammar.explanation: Wh-questions typically fall at the end. "What time is it?" — falling pitch on "is it". The question word itself signals that a specific answer is expected, so the rising pattern of yes/no questions isn't needed.

grammar.sentence: For a list, the intonation pattern is typically: rise-rise-rise-_____.
grammar.hint: Final intonation when list is complete
grammar.explanation: List intonation: rise, rise, rise, FALL. "I need apples, oranges, bananas, and bread" — rising on each item until "bread", which falls to signal "end of list". If the list continued, all items would rise. The falling final = closure.

grammar.sentence: How would you make "Really?" sound like genuine surprise vs sarcasm?
grammar.answer: Surprise: rising-then-rising "Really?" (high pitch). Sarcasm: falling "Really." (low, flat, with stress on first syllable).
grammar.explanation: Same word, two intonations. Genuine surprise rises sharply ("REAL-ly?" high). Sarcastic disbelief falls and flattens ("REAL-ly." low, slow). Intonation carries the emotional content that words alone don't. C2 speakers control this consciously.

grammar.passage: Intonation is the second language inside English. The same words — 'You're going' — can be a statement (falling), a question (rising), an accusation (high pitch on 'YOU'), or a sceptical echo (falling on 'you', rising on 'going'). Without intonation, the words deliver only half their meaning.
grammar.question: According to the passage, how many different meanings can 'You're going' carry through intonation?
grammar.answer: at least four — statement, question, accusation, sceptical echo
grammar.explanation: Four intonation contours for the same words: statement (falling), question (rising), accusation (high on 'YOU'), sceptical echo (falling-rising). Each delivers a different speech act. C2 listeners parse intonation; C2 speakers control it.

units.title: Contractions and elision
units.grammar_focus: Contractions (he's, we'd, won't, shouldn't, mightn't) and elision (drop of /t/ /d/ between consonants — "next month" → "nex' month")
units.real_life_context: You produce the contractions and droppings that fluent English flows on — never speaking entirely "carefully" in conversation.

grammar.sentence: Contraction of "he is going":
grammar.explanation: "He's going" — contraction of "he is". The apostrophe replaces the missing letter. C2 speakers default to contractions in spoken English. Writing without contractions reads as formal or stiff; speaking without contractions reads as foreign.

grammar.sentence: Negative contraction of "should have":
grammar.answer: shouldn't have (often pronounced "shouldn'ta" in casual speech)
grammar.explanation: "Shouldn't have" — standard written contraction of "should not have". In casual fast speech, often produced as "shouldn'ta" /ˈʃʊdn(ə)tə/ — the "have" reduces to a schwa-only sound. C2 listeners parse this; speakers may produce it in casual register.

grammar.sentence: In fast speech, how is "next month" most likely pronounced?
grammar.explanation: Elision: dropping a sound, usually /t/ or /d/, between consonant clusters. "Next month" → "nex' month". Same with "old man" → "ol' man", "first place" → "firs' place". The dropped sound is too hard to say cleanly between adjacent consonants, so native speakers skip it.

grammar.sentence: Native English speaker would most likely say which?
grammar.explanation: "I would have gone if I had known" → casual contracted: "I'd've gone if I'd known". Two contractions stacked: "I'd" (I would) and "'ve" (have). In writing, "I would've" is common; "I'd've" is very informal and mostly spoken. C2 listeners recognise these even when they don't appear in print.

grammar.passage: Native speech is built on contraction and elision. 'Should not have' becomes 'shouldn't've' or 'shouldn'ta'. 'Next month' becomes 'nex' month'. 'Going to' becomes 'gonna'. None of these are lazy — they are the natural sound shape of the language at speed. Speaking only the full forms is the marker of either great formality or great foreignness.
grammar.question: How does the passage describe contractions and elisions?
grammar.answer: as the natural sound shape of the language at speed (not lazy)
grammar.explanation: The point: contracted/elided forms are normal English, not careless English. Native speakers use them constantly; learners who avoid them sound either over-formal or non-native. C2 mastery includes natural use of these forms.

listening_speaking.text: He's been here for two hours.
We'd've left earlier if we could.
Nex' month I'm starting a new job.

cross_unit_consolidation: Stress the correct syllable in multi-syllable words (PHO-tograph vs pho-TO-graphy vs photo-GRAphic)
Distinguish noun-verb pairs by stress (PROduce/proDUCE, REcord/reCORD)
Stress content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) and weaken function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries) — the stress-timed rhythm of English
Produce weak forms with schwa /ə/ for "of", "to", "and", "a", "the"
Link consonant + vowel across word boundaries ("an apple" → "a-napple")
Apply assimilation in casual fast speech ("don't you" → "doncha", "did you" → "didja")
Elide /t/ /d/ in consonant clusters ("next month" → "nex' month")
Choose intonation patterns for function (rising yes/no question, falling wh-question, list rise-rise-rise-fall, falling-flat for sarcasm)
Use contractions and stacked contractions naturally ("he's", "we'd've", "shouldn'ta")
